gmslNote: Global mean sea level from satellite radar altimetry (TOPEX/Poseidon, Jason-1/2/3, Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich; 66S-66N; annual and semi-annual cycles removed; no glacial-isostatic-adjustment correction). Re-zeroed so the 1993 average is 0 mm. About 10-day sampling. Where two satellites overlapped the values were averaged.
annualFallsNote: Years where the annual-mean GMSL fell compared with the year before (from_year, to_year, change_mm): [[1997, 1998, -0.9], [1998, 1999, -0.8], [2010, 2011, -1.7]]

tideGauge.referenceNote: msl_mm = PSMSL RLR annual mean sea level relative to the station's own 1993-2012 mean (7012.4 mm on the RLR scale). This measures sea level relative to the land the gauge sits on. Years with no data (1930, 1941, 2000) are omitted.

ratesDetail.method: Ordinary least-squares straight-line fit of GMSL (mm) against time (years) to all ~10-day values with 1993-01-01 <= t < 2003-01-01 and 2015-01-01 <= t < 2025-01-01. The ols_se values are the naive regression standard errors and ignore autocorrelation, so the true uncertainty is larger.

wmo_state_of_global_climate_2024.source: WMO-No. 1368 State of the Global Climate 2024, https://wmo.int/sites/default/files/2025-03/WMO-1368-2024_en.pdf
wmo_state_of_global_climate_2024.note: Quoted for comparison, not computed here. The NOAA series used in this file gives a smaller increase (about 2.7 to 3.7 mm/yr, up roughly 38%) than the WMO figures (more than doubled). Short-window rates depend on the altimetry processing (for example drift corrections to the early TOPEX/Poseidon data) and on El Nino / La Nina years, so do not mix the two sets of numbers.
